BASIC CUTTING AND TAILORING
11.1 INTRODUCTION
.
The fitting of every garment depends upon the way in which it has been cut and tailored.
And it is essential to have a good drafting and paper pattern. It is important to do a layout
ofthe pattern in order to stitch garments of various designs according to the prevalent
fashion and also forthe effective utilisation of the cloth. Layout is generally used in factories
and a good worker must know have to do a layout. illthis lesson let us learn about layout.
its need, principles and precautions while doing a layout.
11.2
OBJECTIVES
After reading this lesson, you will be able to :
•
'explain the need for a layout;
•
list precautions to be observed while doing a layout;
•
demonstrate the methods of doing layouts ..
11.3 WHAT IS A LAY OUT
Meaning
The marks made on the cloth by laying out the paperpattem keeping in mind the allowances
for the optimum utilisation of cloth, is known as layout.

104 :: Home Science,
11.4 NEED
Wastage of cloth can be avoided by doing a layout. When the cloth is less, it can best
be used by laying out the pattern. Similarly, any spots on the cloth can be avoided by lay
out.
Layout helps to save money. By doing a layout we know exactly how the garment will
.
.
be cut hence there is no wastage.
The checks and print can be matched while doing a layout which saves time later on.
Layout helps in accurate cloth estimation for any garment.
11.5 MARKING
Method of layout
Firstof all,notches andbalance marks aremade on thepattern which has been cutaccording
to the measurements. Layout is the best way of saving cloth and also helps in accurate
cloth estimation.
Lay the pattern on the folded cloth. If the garment is to be front open, then lay the front
piece of the pattern along the selvedge and the back piece on the fold. Mark adequate
)
allowances and turning after laying the front piece. Do-the same for the back piece. After
that lay the sleeve and keep margins all round. In this way the cloth will be cut only after
the entire germent is laid out. Other strips and bias is cut from the left over pieces of
cloth.
If a design is to be added or ajoint is to be shown on the pattern, it must be kept in mind
before hand. In this way, we see that layout helps us to save time and cloth.
11.6 PRECAUTIONS WHILE LAYING OUT
.
1.
Layout should always be done on the wrong side. Be careful to place right side
together.
2.
It is always better to shrink the fabric and then iron it before doing a layout.
3.
Fix the cloth on the table and then layout the pattern and mark it on the cloth.
Then mark the allowances, balance marks, design, etc.

PRECAUTIONS
FOR LAYING OUT ON DIFFERENT
FABRICS
1.
Plain fabric
One has to be careful about the right and wrong side of plain fabrics. The right
side can be identified by the selvedge.
2.
Printed fabric
Extra care has to be taken while doing a layout on printed fabrics. Prints may be
one way prints or all over prints. Care should be taken to see that all lengthwise
pieces are laid out in the same direction specially in one way prints.
•

3.
Striped fabric
One should be careful about the right and wrong side of fabric as well as the
direction of the stripes.Ifthereareuneven stripesthen the stripesshouldbe matched.
If a pocket is to be put on a gents shirt then care should be taken that strips match
exactly.
4.
Piled fabric
Fabrics like velvet and shaneel are piled fabrics. Care should be taken about the
direction of the pile while doing the layout on such fabrics. If the different part of
the garment are cut with different pile directions, the resultant garment will not
look good as the light will be reflected in different directions.
11.7 PRINCIPLE
OF LAY OUT
1.
Check all the components ofthe paper pattern.
2.
Layout the larger parts first and then the smaller ones.
3.
The grain line of the pattern should be laid on the grain line of the fabric.
4.
Adequate margin should be kept between pieces so that they can be cut easily.
5.
Use pins or weights to keep the components of the paper pattern in place.
6.
Mark the outline ofthe paper pattern along the edge of he pattern with a chalk.
7.
Mark the darts, balance marks, turning and seam allowance on the cloth.

11.8 MARGINS
After the layout, margins are kept for turnings, seams, etc. These are as follows -
Inlays
The cloth kept outside the construction line is known as inlay.
Thrning
The cloth kept beyond the full length in order to turn it in and finish the edge is known as
. 'turning allowance'. For example - the round button turning in pants, the round sleeve
turning in shirts, the lower edge turning in frocks, etc.
Margin
The cloth kept apart from seam allowance is known as margin. It is kept at the sides, e.g.
in ladies shirt or in frocks. This margin is kept so that the seam can be opened to increase
the size ofthe gaiment, ifneeded.
Seam allowance
This is the cloth kept for the seams. If the seam allowance has not been marked on the
paper pattern it is marked on the cloth when the pattern is laid out. The seam allowance
may be more or less according to the cloth available.
11.9 FINISIDNG
Finishing refers to neatening the sewed edges by trimming the loose threads and then
pressing. In order to finish a garment the whole should be inspected after completion to
.see which parts need ironing. The garment should be turned inside out to see that all
tacked areas have been sewn properly and the tacks removed. Shake the garment well
so that any loose threads sticking to it are shaken out. If necessary, they may be brushed
out with the help of abrush. If paper has been used during garment construction that too
must be carefully removed.
A second inspection ofthe garment should be done after finishing it to see that no part
has been left unstitched or ifthe seam at any place is so near the edge that it is likely to
fray very soon. Corrective measures should be taken in such cases.
The last stage in finishing ispressing the garment properly sothat it looks attractive. Hence,
finishing agarment after stitching is very important.
